Empirical Research Plan ‑ PANES, Political Support & Persistence

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Identification Strategy
──────────────────────────
Method: Local Sharp / Fuzzy Regression-Discontinuity Design (RDD) combined with repeat-measurement (2006/07 and 2008) to study immediate and persistent effects.

Why RDD?  
• Eligibility for PANES is a deterministic, secret, single-index rule with a known cutoff.  
• Households cannot precisely manipulate the confidential score ⇒ potential outcomes should be smooth at the threshold.  
• We observe the running variable and can restrict the sample to a narrow ±2 pp window supplied by MIDES, creating quasi-random assignment.  
• Two post-program survey waves allow us to estimate:  
  – Short-run LATE (2006/07)  
  – Medium-run LATE (2008, after transfers ended)  
  – Compare both to speak to persistence and mechanisms.

Sharp vs. Fuzzy:  If compliance with the cutoff is ≈100 %, we treat it as sharp; if not, we instrument “ever-received PANES” with “eligibility” in a fuzzy RD (FRD).  The code template below implements FRD.

Optional extension: “Local difference-in-differences” that adds the 2005 baseline outcome as a control to improve precision and relax the parallel-trend concern for persistence results.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2. Treatment and Control Definition
───────────────────────────────────
• Running variable (R): Confidential predicted-income score (lower = poorer).  
• Cutoff (c): Official PANES eligibility threshold (R ≤ c ⇒ eligible).  

Treatment variable (T):  
  Tᵢ = 1 if household ever received at least one PANES cash payment (administrative data).

Control group:  
  Households with R just above the cutoff (R > c) that never received PANES.

Timing:  
  – Program starts April 2005.  
  – First follow-up survey Oct 2006–Mar 2007 (during transfers).  
  – Second follow-up Feb–Mar 2008 (after program ended).  

We estimate separate RDs for each survey wave as well as a stacked specification with a wave indicator to test persistence.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
──────────────────────────────
A1. Continuity of potential outcomes at the cutoff.  
     Plausibility: Score was secret; no evidence applicants knew the formula. Economic/political attitudes should evolve smoothly in the narrow window absent treatment.

A2. No precise manipulation of the running variable (no “gaming”).  
     Plausibility: External academics designed the formula; documentation suggests households could not observe or influence the score ex-ante. We will test with McCrary density.

A3. Single treatment discontinuity.  
     Plausibility: No other large programs used the same score in 2005–07. The 2008 Plan de Equidad did not depend on the original score within the ±2 pp band and enrolled similar shares of both sides ⇒ unlikely to confound persistence estimates.

A4. Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA) locally.  
     Plausibility: Spillovers across near-cutoff households are minimal—the cash transfer averaged only 10 % of median income, unlikely to shift neighborhood-level politics.

A5. Survey non-response/attrition is independent of eligibility within the window.  
     Plausibility: Follow-up rates are high (>80 %); we will check balance and use inverse-probability weights if needed.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
──────────────────────────────────────────
T1. Manipulation of the score.  
    • Test: McCrary density & covariate smoothness.  
    • Mitigate: If manipulation detected, adopt narrower bandwidths and/or donut RDD (drop ±0.1 pp around c).

T2. Differential sample selection / attrition.  
    • Compare baseline covariates & response rates by eligibility.  
    • Use IPW or Lee bounds to bracket estimates.

T3. Contamination from Plan de Equidad (2008).  
    • Show that enrollment in the 2008 program is smooth at c.  
    • Include indicator “received Plan de Equidad” as a control in 2008 regressions.  
    • Interpret 2008 estimates as “intent-to-treat” persistence net of subsequent common benefits.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
5. R Code Outline
──────────────────
```r
# 0. Libraries -------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)      # fast data wrangling
library(fixest)          # regressions
library(rdrobust)        # RD estimation
library(ggplot2)         # plots

# 1. Load & merge data -----------------------------------------------------
# Assume three csvs: baseline_2005.csv, followup_2006.csv, followup_2008.csv
base  <- fread("baseline_2005.csv")
f06   <- fread("followup_2006.csv")
f08   <- fread("followup_2008.csv")

# Harmonise variable names & bind
all <- rbindlist(list(
        cbind(f06, wave = 1),
        cbind(f08, wave = 2)
      ), use.names = TRUE, fill = TRUE)

# 2. Variable construction -------------------------------------------------
all[, treat      := ever_received_panes]           # 1/0 admin
all[, eligible   := as.integer(score <= cutoff)]  # forcing variable
all[, running    := score - cutoff]               # centred variable
all[, support_FA := as.integer(support_current_gov == 1)]  # 1 = supports FA
all[, after_prog := (wave == 2)]                  # post-PANES indicator

# 3. Main RD (wave-specific) ----------------------------------------------
# Fuzzy RD: outcome on eligibility, instrumenting treat with eligible
rd_2006 <- rdrobust(y = all[wave==1]$support_FA,
                    x = all[wave==1]$running,
                    c = 0, fuzzy = all[wave==1]$treat,
                    p = 1)
rd_2008 <- rdrobust(y = all[wave==2]$support_FA,
                    x = all[wave==2]$running,
                    c = 0, fuzzy = all[wave==2]$treat,
                    p = 1)

# 4. Persistence test in stacked data -------------------------------------
stack_mod <- feols(support_FA ~ treat*after_prog | 0 | treat ~ eligible,
                   data = all[abs(running)<=0.02])  # 2-pp window
# Report first-stage F, ITT and LATE (2SLS) automatically

# 5. Robustness: Donut RDD & Covariate balance -----------------------------
# Donut: drop ±0.001 around cutoff
donut <- all[abs(running) > 0.001 & abs(running) <= 0.02 & wave==1]
rd_donut <- rdrobust(y = donut$support_FA,
                     x = donut$running,
                     c = 0, fuzzy = donut$treat)

# Covariate balance example
covars <- c("hhsize","head_age","female_head","urban")
bal_results <- lapply(covars, function(v){
    rdrobust(y = all[[v]], x = all$running, c = 0)
})
```

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
6. Expected Results
────────────────────
Economic reasoning and previous literature on cash transfers suggest a gratitude/reciprocity effect plus updating about the left-wing coalition’s redistributive preference.

Prior:  
• Short-run: treated households’ probability of supporting the incumbent FA rises by ~10-15 percentage points (pp) relative to mean support of ~45 % in the control group.  
• Persistence: effect attenuates but remains positive at ~5–7 pp one year after transfers ceased, indicating partial but not full decay.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (RDD)
───────────────────────────────────────────
C1. No manipulation of running variable density ………………… 1  
C2. Covariate continuity at cutoff ……………………………… 1  
C3. Correct functional form / bandwidth choice ……………… 1  
C4. No other discontinuous treatments at cutoff ……………… 0.8  
C5. Stable survey participation across cutoff ………………… 0.8  

(Overall: 4.6 / 5 ≈ “highly credible,” with minor caution on C4–C5.)

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
This plan leverages the sharp eligibility rule to obtain credible causal effects of PANES on political attitudes and their persistence, while explicitly testing and adjusting for the primary threats to identification.
